verdict: Avoid new wholesale-trade exposure in Delhi for now; lend only to fast-moving, cash-and-carry distributors with tight stock-and-receivable discipline, and decline festive-dependent discretionary traders.
title: Delhi Wholesale Trade: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Delhi wholesale is a working-capital business, not an asset business.** Traders in Chandni Chowk, Sadar Bazaar, Khari Baoli and Chawri Bazaar buy stock, hold it briefly, and sell to buyers who travel in from neighbouring cities — around three to four lakh buyers daily and nearly 5,000 goods vehicles entering the area [2]. Cash is made on turnover and margin per cycle, not on fixed assets, so the loan is really financing inventory and receivables. **CRISIL flags receivables and inventory as the two risks that decide a trader's fate** — collection efficiency and obsolescence, especially in garments and fast-moving consumer goods [9][10]. So when a proposal lands, check receivable days against the trader's own three-year history, not the industry average; if receivables are stretching while sales are flat, ask why stock is still being bought.

## What has changed now
**Delhi's local demand is running behind India.** GST collections are up 2.7% Apr-to-date against India's 6.1%, and electricity demand up 6.5% against 9.5% [D] — both local stress signals. On top of that, the 1 November INDIA bloc rally shut roughly 80% of shops in 20-22 major markets, with CTI estimating a Rs 10,000-12,000 crore business hit and noting Rs 25,000 crore of goods normally bought on Dhanteras alone [1][2][3]. **That is a festive-season cash-flow shock, and festive stock is often bought on borrowed money.** Nationally, bank credit is growing 29.1% against activity of 6.1% [D], so money is chasing traders faster than their sales — a recipe for stretched receivables. The repo at 5.5%, raised from 5.25% with a tightening stance [D], means the cost of carrying that stock is rising.

## Where the growth is
**Pursue distributors of everyday, fast-moving goods — staples, FMCG, pharmacy, hardware — where buyers reorder monthly and stock turns quickly.** Peer evidence supports wholesale as a live channel: Aditya Birla Lifestyle's wholesale channel grew 18% in Q2FY27 [7], and Mishka Exim's June 2026 net sales rose 234.87% year on year on jewellery and fabrics trading, though at an 11.5% gross margin [5]. **Avoid festive-dependent, discretionary and high-obsolescence traders** — garments, electronics, giftware — who carry the rally loss and the stock-risk CRISIL warns about [9].

## How to grow safely
**Structure every limit against the working-capital cycle, not the balance sheet.** Take monthly stock statements and receivable ageing; require receivables within the trader's own historical range [10]. Ask for cash-flow statements showing festive-season collections, and if the trader cannot produce them, collect from customer. **Price the higher repo into the limit** [D].

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for stock building while sales slow, and for buyers from outside Delhi cancelling visits** — CTI already reports out-of-town buyers cancelling [2]. If receivable days cross the trader's three-year high, cut the limit.

## What I want you to do this month
**Pull the top ten wholesale exposures and rank them by receivable days and stock turns.** Any name where receivables have stretched beyond its own three-year high goes to me before renewal. **The data call is Avoid; treat this book as a watch-and-shrink exercise until Delhi's GST and power numbers close the gap with India** [D].
watch: Receivable days above the trader's three-year high -> freeze fresh limits and ask for collection plan
Delhi GST growth stays below India's 6.1% for two more prints -> stop new sanctions in the segment [D]
Sales below the trader's own prior-year festive figure -> re-rate limit down and seek collateral
Buyer footfall and goods-vehicle movement in the wholesale markets (weekly)
Sustained drop in out-of-town buyers -> shift to cash-and-carry distributors only [2]
Repo above 5.5% or credit gap widening -> reprice limits and shorten tenors [D]
